title: From the Great Sphinx’s Raw Materials, a New Crocodile Species Surfaces - Nautilus
author: Devin Reese
text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementZoologyFrom the Great Sphinx’s Raw Materials, a New Crocodile Species SurfacesIt from a bygone epoch when all sorts of crocs roamed the MediterraneanDRBy Devin Reese6:00 PM CDT on October 6, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleOne of Egypt’s most iconic reminders of the Old Kingdom is the Great Sphinx, which was carved right out of the Giza Plateau’s limestone bedrock, a collection of ancient seabed sediments that accumulated at the bottom of what was then the warm, shallow Tethys Sea. That same material—from the Mokattam Formation east of Cairo—has now yielded a new species of crocodile: Herugavialis cairensis.According to a study published this evening in the journal Royal Society Open Science, a team of researchers from the U.K., Sweden, Germany, and Egypt determined that Herugavialis cairensis’ skull shape marked it as “gavial,” or a fish-eating crocodile characterized by a long, skinny snout. Only this one was missing the tip—or at least the fossilized remainder of it. “Given this coincidence with the famously missing nose of the Great Sphinx, we decided to name the new crocodile after the Egyptian god Heru,” explained lead study author Paul Burke, a paleobiologist at University College London. Its fossil bones had previously led paleontologists to identify it as another ancient gavial from Egypt: Tomistoma cairense. But the study authors got a deeper look at the skull by CT-scanning it and found differences that warranted the new species classification. For example, its bony eye sockets protruded out from its skull like the opening of a telescope, and its cheek bone (“squamosal”) was a strip shape rather than a wedge.Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisement
